person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the methods available for studying perceptual decisions in mice and rats, and whether they can reach the rigour established in primate psychophysics
span.quote: However, rigorous psychophysical methods are not yet as developed for these rodents as they are for primates.

span.label: can perceptual decision-making be probed in rodents to a standard comparable with primates, and what does each task design let one conclude
span.quote: Understanding the underlying processes and their neural bases requires that one pair recordings and manipulations of neural activity with rigorous psychophysics.

span.label: sets out what each rodent task design can and cannot rule out, and corrects two widely held beliefs about rodents that turn out to be artefacts of laboratory practice
span.quote: These methods represent a rich set of challenges and opportunities.

span.label: method
span.quote: We then review methods of psychophysics, focusing on the technical issues that arise in their implementation in rodents.

span.label: perceptual decision-making in rodents
span.quote: Here we review some of the techniques for studying perceptual decisions in rodents.

span.label: review
span.quote: Here we give a brief overview of the sensory capabilities of rodents and of their cortical areas devoted to sensation and decision.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a shift in decision criterion or in willingness to act inflates the response rate, which is then misread as an improvement in the neural representation of the stimulus
span.quote: It would be premature to conclude that the optogenetic stimulation enhanced the neural representation of the tone: the increased response rate might simply reflect an increased willingness to perform the response action or to report the tone's presence, for instance because of a change in decision criterion.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: free water over the weekend leaves animals under-motivated at the start of the week, which drives the observed day-of-week variation in trial counts and proficiency
span.quote: However, this regime causes substantial variations in motivation across days of the week, with the animals being insufficiently motivated and proficient early in the week.

span.label: a belief about the animal is traced back to how the animal is kept: mice look nocturnal because laboratory food is unlimited
span.quote: The view of mice as minimally visual might stem from the belief that they are nocturnal. Mice, however, are reliably nocturnal only if food is unlimited, as is typical in the laboratory; when food is scarcer, they sleep part of the night to lower body temperature and conserve energy

span.label: the correction is checked against morphology rather than behaviour alone - the eyes lack the tapetum a nocturnal animal would have
span.quote: In nature, indeed, laboratory mice can become entirely diurnal 27 . Accordingly, the eyes of rats and mice lack the reflective tapetum that would be expected in nocturnal animals.

span.label: task designs are ordered by what each one can rule out, so the choice of design is presented as a choice of which confound survives
span.quote: Unlike a go/no-go task, however, this design is immune to changes in a subject's willingness to respond, because the subject must report a decision on every trial. The requirement to respond on every trial, likewise, makes it clearer which responses constitute true decisions.

span.label: the criterion problem is made concrete with a hypothetical optogenetic result that would be misread under a go/no-go design
span.quote: Moreover, suppose one used a go/no-go design to compare a mouse's ability to detect a faint tone, with and without optogenetic stimulation. Suppose further that the stimulation increased the percentage of time the mouse indicated the presence of the tone. It would be premature to conclude that the optogenetic stimulation enhanced the neural representation of the tone: the increased response rate might simply reflect an increased willingness to perform the response action or to report the tone's presence, for instance because of a change in decision criterion.

span.label: d-prime is preferred over the raw hit-minus-false-alarm difference specifically because the latter moves when only the criterion moves
span.quote: This measure is preferable to the difference between correct detections and false alarms (which has been used in some studies, e.g. 67 ), because the latter can change markedly following simple changes in criterion

span.label: a two-stimulus design removes the criterion entirely, because presence must be assigned to one location and absence to the other
span.quote: Indeed, in a task with two stimulus presentations subjects cannot have a bias for the presence or absence of a stimulus attribute: in each choice they must assign presence to a location and absence to the other.

span.label: one stimulus intensity is shown to be uninterpretable: sensitivity, bias and lapse rate produce identical data at a single point
span.quote: Obtaining behavioral data at only a single intensity (as is often done in rodent studies) would not allow one to distinguish the effects of sensitivity, bias, and lapse rate.

span.label: the fix is a full psychometric curve, whose slope, position and tails separate the three
span.quote: In the classic psychophysical approach, one presents stimuli of multiple intensities to obtain a full psychometric function ( Fig. 3 a ). The steepness of this function measures perceptual sensitivity; its horizontal position measures sensory bias, and the levels of its tails is a measure of guessing (lapse rate), which reflects quality of training and degree of engagement.

span.label: short training is argued against on the grounds that error trials become uninterpretable, since a mistake may be about the stimulus or about the task
span.quote: Errors are difficult to interpret during early stages of training: they may reflect confusion about the stimulus (“was that tone high or low?”) or confusion about the task (“what am I supposed to do for high tones?

span.label: a well-trained animal makes error trials interpretable, and near-perfect performance on easy trials is the check that the task itself is understood
span.quote: Therefore, neural activity recorded during an error trial in a well-trained animal can be confidently interpreted as reflecting misperception of the stimulus.

span.label: an unpublished four-fold day-of-week effect on trial count is reported, traced to the weekend water schedule
span.quote: The difference can be as large as a factor of 4, with mice performing ~100 trials/session on Mondays vs. ~400 trials/session on Fridays (M.C., unpublished observations).

span.label: the tacit knowledge attached to a standard task is named as knowledge that circulates informally and appears in no paper
span.quote: Those researchers have developed a shared and informal knowledge of this task's properties and the strategies it elicits. For instance, they know that one must present a balance of easy and difficult stimuli to discourage strategies where the animals selectively discard trials that are too hard.

span.label: The authors state that their own background biases the review toward one brain region and one modality.
span.quote: Finally, due to our own backgrounds and interests, we perhaps unduly emphasize one brain region, the cerebral cortex, and one sensory modality, vision.

span.label: The review is framed around unresolved questions rather than settled answers about rodent perceptual ability.
span.quote: We highlight what are mainly open questions about rodent perceptual abilities and our ability to assess these experimentally.

span.label: The widely held view that rats out-train mice is flagged by the authors as untested.
span.quote: As far as we know, however, this view has not been directly tested.

span.label: the widely held view that rats out-learn mice has never been directly tested
span.quote: As far as we know, however, this view has not been directly tested.

span.label: and may be an artefact of training technique rather than a species difference
span.quote: In fact, rats may only appear to be easier to train simply because mice require different training techniques. Once optimal training procedures are developed for mice, their cognitive abilities may prove to rival those of rats.

span.label: a term the field uses to justify design decisions has no agreed definition
span.quote: The notion of “overtraining”, however, is poorly defined.

span.label: whether longer training adds more uncontrolled plasticity than shorter training is not established either way
span.quote: Perhaps longer training schedules elicit more unwanted and uncontrolled plasticity than shorter ones, but it is not clear that this plasticity would complicate interpretation of behavioral and neural data more than the plasticity induced by shorter training schedules.

span.label: virtual environments lack vestibular feedback, which visual feedback may not compensate for
span.quote: Further, the visual feedback in the virtual environment may not entirely make up for the lack of vestibular feedback.

span.label: rodents should not be treated as a replacement for primates
span.quote: For this and other reasons, including the closer similarity with the human brain, it would be a mistake to consider rodents as a complete replacement for primates in investigations of perceptual decision-making.

span.label: whether rodent designs can reach primate psychophysical rigour is left open
span.quote: First, will a few sensory environments be adopted as industry standards or will multiple environments be used in parallel? Second, will experimental designs in rodents be able to take advantage of rigorous psychophysical methods, as much as those that were developed for primates?

span.label: punishment-based training learns fast but may induce stress that blocks harder tasks
span.quote: These methods may be advantageous as they can lead to very fast learning of simple tasks, but they may create stress, which might prevent learning of more complex tasks.

span.label: the whole task toolbox - random-dot motion, forced choice, psychometric curves - carried into rodents together with the standards for interpreting it
span.quote: However, rigorous psychophysical methods are not yet as developed for these rodents as they are for primates.

span.label: the separation of sensitivity from criterion, imported as the reason a rodent task must measure false alarms and not only hits
span.quote: In SDT, one measures not only the rate of correct detections, but also the rate of false alarms: trials where the animal reported the stimulus or attribute was present when it wasn't. These rates yield a measure of detectability called d ', which is independent of criterion, and thus immune to its changes.

span.label: the mouse as a nocturnal, minimally visual animal versus as a facultatively diurnal one - the first turns out to be an artefact of unlimited laboratory food
span.quote: The view of mice as minimally visual might stem from the belief that they are nocturnal. Mice, however, are reliably nocturnal only if food is unlimited, as is typical in the laboratory; when food is scarcer, they sleep part of the night to lower body temperature and conserve energy

span.label: detectability - as the raw difference between hits and false alarms versus as d-prime, which is criterion-independent; the two diverge whenever the criterion moves
span.quote: This measure is preferable to the difference between correct detections and false alarms (which has been used in some studies, e.g. 67 ), because the latter can change markedly following simple changes in criterion

span.label: a performance change - as reduced sensitivity, as shifted bias, or as raised lapse rate; three distinct mechanisms indistinguishable at a single stimulus intensity
span.quote: A tempting interpretation is that the manipulation decreased the subject's sensitivity ( Fig. 3 b ). However, two other changes would lead to identical changes at that stimulus strength: a change in bias ( Fig. 3 c ) and a change in lapse rate

span.label: two-alternative choice (one stimulus, two responses) versus two-alternative forced choice (two stimuli, two responses) - names that are often conflated and designs that differ in exactly which confound they remove
span.quote: A further refinement of the experimental design, used in a few rodent studies 31 , 40 , 72 – 74 involves presenting not one but two stimuli (simultaneously or in succession) and asking the subject which of the two has the attribute in question. This design is called “forced choice” or (since the choice is between two stimuli), “two-alternative forced choice

span.label: an error trial - as misperception of the stimulus versus as confusion about the task; only training separates them
span.quote: Errors are difficult to interpret during early stages of training: they may reflect confusion about the stimulus (“was that tone high or low?”) or confusion about the task (“what am I supposed to do for high tones?

span.label: a species difference in trainability versus a difference in the training techniques that happen to have been developed
span.quote: In fact, rats may only appear to be easier to train simply because mice require different training techniques. Once optimal training procedures are developed for mice, their cognitive abilities may prove to rival those of rats.

span.label: rodent frontal cortex as fundamentally different from primate on histological grounds versus as functionally equivalent on behavioural grounds
span.quote: Rodent frontal cortex has been the subject of debate: some have argued, based on histology, that frontal regions are fundamentally different in primate and rodents

span.label: critiques → the view that rodent behaviour is only weakly influenced by vision
span.quote: A notion that might be flawed, however, is that rodent behavior is only weakly influenced by vision.

span.label: contradicts → the belief that mice are nocturnal, which the paper traces to unlimited laboratory food
span.quote: This evidence, contradicts the view that mice are nocturnal, a fact that has consequences for the design and interpretation of behavioral experiments.

span.label: critiques → rodent studies that measure behaviour at a single stimulus intensity
span.quote: Obtaining behavioral data at only a single intensity (as is often done in rodent studies) would not allow one to distinguish the effects of sensitivity, bias, and lapse rate.

span.label: critiques → the untested consensus that rats learn perceptual tasks faster than mice
span.quote: As far as we know, however, this view has not been directly tested.

span.label: critiques → the use of the difference between hit and false-alarm rates as a detectability measure
span.quote: This measure is preferable to the difference between correct detections and false alarms (which has been used in some studies, e.g. 67 ), because the latter can change markedly following simple changes in criterion

span.label: builds-on → primate psychophysics, whose task toolbox and standards the paper takes as the benchmark
span.quote: However, rigorous psychophysical methods are not yet as developed for these rodents as they are for primates.

span.label: supports → evidence that rodent frontal cortex, like primate, supports working memory and categorization, against the histological argument for fundamental difference
span.quote: However, emerging evidence suggests that frontal cortex in rodents, as in primates, is essential for higher cognitive functions including working memory and categorization

span.label: Signal Detection Theory —contrasted-with→ Drift Diffusion Model
span.quote: An increasingly popular alternative to SDT, the Drift Diffusion Model 2 postulates a decision variable that drifts in one direction or the other depending on the accumulating evidence. When the variable crosses a threshold, it triggers a decision. This model captures not only a subject's accuracy, but also the time required to respond.

span.label: Posterior Parietal Cortex —causes→ evidence integration
span.quote: A cortical area that appears to play an intriguing role in decision-making is the Posterior Parietal Cortex (PPC, labeled PTLp in Fig. 1 b ). First, in rodents as in primates, PPC lies at the heart of a network of sensory areas, receiving inputs from auditory, visual and somatosensory areas 34 , 35 ; it is therefore poised to integrate multisensory inputs.

span.label: lapse rate —part-of→ psychometric curves
span.quote: In the classic psychophysical approach, one presents stimuli of multiple intensities to obtain a full psychometric function ( Fig. 3 a ). span.label: Go/no-go designs, the most common choice in rodent work, confound perceptual ability with the animal's motivation and response criterion.
span.quote: A key issue with go/no-go tasks is that they are highly vulnerable to changes in the animal's motivation and criterion.

span.label: Requiring a response on every trial removes the confound of a changing willingness to respond, though not the confound of a changing criterion.
span.quote: Unlike a go/no-go task, however, this design is immune to changes in a subject's willingness to respond, because the subject must report a decision on every trial.

span.label: Presenting two stimuli and asking which carries the attribute is the only design immune to an unknown, drifting decision criterion, because the subject cannot be biased toward presence or absence.
span.quote: in a task with two stimulus presentations subjects cannot have a bias for the presence or absence of a stimulus attribute: in each choice they must assign presence to a location and absence to the other.

span.label: Testing at only one stimulus strength, as rodent studies commonly do, makes a change in sensitivity indistinguishable from a change in bias or in lapse rate, so causal manipulations cannot be interpreted.
span.quote: Obtaining behavioral data at only a single intensity (as is often done in rodent studies) would not allow one to distinguish the effects of sensitivity, bias, and lapse rate.

span.label: The widespread assumption that mice are nocturnal is an artefact of unlimited laboratory food, and their eyes lack the anatomical signature of nocturnal animals.
